domain.title: Numerics & Precision
domain.tag: IEEE 754 · error analysis · bf16 & fp8 · quantisation · determinism
domain.why: Computers don't store numbers perfectly — they approximate them, and every approximation can quietly go wrong in ways that don't announce themselves. A rounding choice that seems tiny can make an AI model fail to train at all, or make two 'identical' calculations give different answers depending on how the work was split up. This domain is about the actual bit patterns underneath the numbers, not just trusting that arithmetic works.

sections.note: the bit layout is the whole subject; every surprise later in this domain is a consequence of it

concepts.t: The three fields: sign, exponent, significand

L0.body:
# binary32: 1 sign | 8 exponent | 23 stored significand bits
>>> import struct
>>> struct.unpack('>I', struct.pack('>f', 1.0))[0]
1065353216                       # 0x3F800000 = 0 01111111 00000000000000000000000
>>> struct.unpack('>I', struct.pack('>f', 0.1))[0]
1036831949                       # 0x3DCCCCCD = 0 01111011 10011001100110011001101
# value = (-1)^s * 1.f * 2^(E - bias)      for 0 < E < all-ones
L0.cloze: binary32 is {{c1::1}} sign bit, {{c2::8}} exponent bits and {{c3::23}} stored significand bits; the value of a normal number is {{c4::$(-1)^{s} \cdot 1.f \cdot 2^{E-\text{bias}}$}}.

concepts.L1: A binary float is three integer fields packed into one word: a sign bit, a biased exponent, and a fixed-width significand. binary16 is 1/5/10, binary32 is 1/8/23, binary64 is 1/11/52. The exponent buys range; the significand buys precision.
concepts.L2: The split is a budget, not a hierarchy. Adding an exponent bit doubles the number of binades you can reach and costs you one significand bit, halving precision everywhere. Every ML format argument — bf16 against fp16, E4M3 against E5M2 — is that one trade made again at a smaller width.
concepts.L3: Decode $0x3DCCCCCD$ by hand. Sign $0$. Exponent field $01111011_{2} = 123$, so the unbiased exponent is $123 - 127 = -4$. Stored significand $10011001100110011001101_{2}$, prefixed with the implicit one, gives $1.6000000238418579$. The value is $1.6000000238418579 \times 2^{-4} = 0.100000001490116$, not $0.1$: one tenth is $0.0\overline{0011}$ in binary, an infinite repeating expansion, so it is not representable in any binary format at any width. The stored bits are the closest 24-bit truncation, rounded up at the last bit — which is why the pattern ends in $\ldots 1101$ and not $\ldots 1100$.

L4.prompt_tpl: How many bits does the significand field store in binary{w}, and how many bits of precision does the significand actually have?
L4.answer: binary16: 10 stored, 11 effective. binary32: 23 stored, 24 effective. binary64: 52 stored, 53 effective. Effective = stored + 1 for the implicit leading one (normals only).
L4.explanation: Computed from the interchange-format table. Precision $p$ = stored bits + 1 because normals carry an implicit leading $1$. This is why fp32 is quoted as 24-bit precision and $\log_{10}(2^{24}) \approx 7.22$ decimal digits.

L4.prompt_tpl: What is the exact fp32 bit pattern of {v}, in hex?
L4.explanation: Verified with struct.pack('>f', v). Powers of two have an all-zero significand, so only the sign and exponent fields change: $1.0$ is exponent field $127$, $2.0$ is $128$, $0.5$ is $126$. Flipping the sign bit alone turns $2.0$ into $-2.0$.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why 0.1 has no exact representation in any binary floating-point format.
L4.answer: A binary float is $m \cdot 2^{e}$ with integer $m$; such a number has only $2$ in its denominator in lowest terms. $1/10 = 1/(2 \cdot 5)$ has a factor of $5$, so no finite $m, e$ can produce it.
L4.explanation: The decidable rule: a rational $p/q$ in lowest terms is exactly representable in base $b$ iff every prime factor of $q$ divides $b$. Base 2 admits only $q = 2^{k}$. This is why $0.1 + 0.2 \neq 0.3$ and why money is not stored in binary floats.

L0.body:
# bias = 2^(w-1) - 1  for an exponent field of width w
#   binary16  w=5   bias=15     E in [1,30]  -> e in [-14, 15]
#   binary32  w=8   bias=127    E in [1,254] -> e in [-126, 127]
#   binary64  w=11  bias=1023   E in [1,2046]-> e in [-1022, 1023]
# E = 0            -> subnormal / zero  (e = 1 - bias, NOT -bias)
# E = all ones     -> infinity / NaN
>>> (1 << (8-1)) - 1
127
L0.cloze: The exponent bias for a width-$w$ field is {{c1::$2^{w-1} - 1$}}; for binary32 that is {{c2::127}}. Field value $0$ means {{c3::subnormal or zero}} and all-ones means {{c4::infinity or NaN}}.

concepts.L1: The exponent is stored as an unsigned integer with a constant subtracted off, so no sign bit or two's complement is needed inside it. Bias is $2^{w-1}-1$: 15 for binary16, 127 for binary32, 1023 for binary64.
concepts.L2: The bias is $2^{w-1}-1$ and not $2^{w-1}$ so that the two reserved codes bracket the range asymmetrically and, more usefully, so that the bit pattern of a positive float compares correctly as an unsigned integer. Sorting an array of non-negative fp32 values as uint32 gives exactly the float order.
concepts.L3: Two consequences fall out of biased storage. First, monotonicity: because sign is the top bit and the exponent sits directly below the significand in the word, for non-negative floats $x \leq y$ if and only if $\mathrm{bits}(x) \leq \mathrm{bits}(y)$ as unsigned integers. Radix-sorting floats and the classic $\mathrm{nextafter}$ implementation (add one to the integer) both rely on this. Second, the exponent range is not symmetric: binary32 reaches $e = 127$ up but only $e = -126$ down, because $E = 0$ was spent on subnormals. So $\mathrm{fp32max} \approx 3.40 \times 10^{38}$ while the smallest normal is $1.175 \times 10^{-38}$ — their product is not 1.

L4.prompt_tpl: An exponent field is {w} bits wide. Give the bias, and the largest and smallest exponent available to normal numbers. Answer with the bias.
L4.explanation: Computed from the closed form. Field values $0$ and all-ones are reserved, so normals use $E \in [1, 2^{w}-2]$, giving $e = E - \mathrm{bias} \in [1-\mathrm{bias}, \mathrm{bias}]$. Note fp8 E4M3 breaks this: it reclaims the all-ones exponent, so $e_{\max} = 8$, not 7.

L4.prompt_tpl: You reinterpret two non-negative float{w} values as unsigned integers and compare them. What happens?
options: The integer comparison always agrees with the float comparison
The comparison is correct only when both have the same exponent
The comparison is reversed for values below 1.0
L4.answer: The integer comparison always agrees with the float comparison
L4.explanation: Biased exponent above significand, both unsigned, means the concatenation is monotone in the value. This is why $\mathrm{nextafter}$ can be implemented as an integer increment, and why float radix sort works. It fails once negatives are involved, since the sign bit inverts the order of the rest.

L0.body:
# Normal numbers: significand is 1.f, the leading 1 is NOT stored.
#   1.0 fp32 = 0x3F800000 -> significand field is all zeros, value is 1.000...0
# You get 24 bits of precision out of 23 stored bits. Free bit.
#
# The price: 1.f cannot represent anything below 2^emin.
#   E = 0 is the escape hatch -> significand reads 0.f instead (subnormal)
>>> import numpy as np
>>> np.float32(1.0).view(np.uint32)      # 0x3F800000, mantissa field == 0
np.uint32(1065353216)
L0.cloze: For normal numbers the significand is read as {{c1::$1.f$}} with the leading one {{c2::not stored}}, so binary32 gets {{c3::24}} bits of precision from 23 stored bits. When the exponent field is {{c4::0}} the significand is read as $0.f$ instead.

concepts.L1: Every normalised binary number has exactly one leading 1 before the radix point, so storing it is a waste. IEEE 754 omits it and reconstructs it during decode. Precision is stored bits plus one.
concepts.L2: The free bit is not free everywhere: it is precisely why subnormals need a separate encoding. Once $1.f \geq 1$ is hardwired, no bit pattern can name a value below $2^{e_{\min}}$, so the standard reserves $E = 0$ to switch the interpretation to $0.f$ with exponent $1 - \mathrm{bias}$ rather than $-\mathrm{bias}$.
concepts.L3: The off-by-one in the subnormal exponent is the detail people get wrong. With $E = 0$ the exponent is $1 - \mathrm{bias}$, not $0 - \mathrm{bias}$, so the subnormal range abuts the normal range with no gap: the largest subnormal is $(1 - 2^{-23}) \times 2^{-126}$ and the smallest normal is $1.0 \times 2^{-126}$, one ulp apart. Had the standard used $-\mathrm{bias}$, there would be a factor-of-two hole at the boundary. Consequence: in fp32, $2^{24} + 1$ is not representable. The exact sum needs 25 significand bits and you only have 24, so round-to-nearest returns $2^{24}$ and $x + 1 == x$ becomes true at $16777216$.

L4.prompt_tpl: In binary{w}, what is the smallest positive integer n such that n + 1 is not exactly representable?
L4.explanation: Integers are exact while they fit in $p$ significand bits. At $2^{p}$ the spacing becomes $2$, so odd integers vanish. Verified: np.float16(2048)+np.float16(1) returns 2048.0 and np.float32(2**24)+np.float32(1) returns 16777216.0. This is why token counts and step counters belong in int64.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why is the subnormal exponent defined as 1 - bias rather than 0 - bias?
L4.answer: So the subnormal and normal ranges join with uniform spacing. The largest subnormal (1 - 2^-m) * 2^(1-bias) is exactly one ulp below the smallest normal 1.0 * 2^(1-bias). Using -bias would open a factor-of-two gap.
L4.explanation: This is the definition that makes underflow gradual rather than abrupt. Check it in fp32: largest subnormal $1.17549421 \times 10^{-38}$, smallest normal $1.17549435 \times 10^{-38}$, difference $1.4 \times 10^{-45}$, which is exactly the subnormal spacing $2^{-149}$.

L0.body:
>>> import numpy as np, struct
>>> struct.unpack('>f', struct.pack('>I', 0x00800000))[0]   # smallest NORMAL
1.1754943508222875e-38
>>> struct.unpack('>f', struct.pack('>I', 0x007FFFFF))[0]   # largest SUBNORMAL
1.1754942106924411e-38
>>> struct.unpack('>f', struct.pack('>I', 0x00000001))[0]   # smallest SUBNORMAL
1.401298464324817e-45
# subnormal value = 0.f * 2^(1-bias) = f * 2^(emin - m)
# fp16: min normal 6.103515625e-05, min subnormal 5.960464477539063e-08
L0.cloze: When the exponent field is zero the significand is read as {{c1::$0.f$}} with exponent {{c2::$1-\mathrm{bias}$}}. These are {{c3::subnormal}} numbers and they give {{c4::gradual}} underflow, at the cost of losing precision as the value shrinks.

concepts.L1: Subnormals fill the gap between zero and the smallest normal with evenly spaced values of decreasing precision. In fp32 they run from $1.4 \times 10^{-45}$ to $1.175 \times 10^{-38}$; in fp16 from $5.96 \times 10^{-8}$ to $6.10 \times 10^{-5}$.
concepts.L2: They exist to make $x - y = 0$ imply $x = y$. Without subnormals, two distinct normals closer than $2^{e_{\min}}$ subtract to a value that must flush to zero, and that guarantee — the one every convergence test assumes — breaks. GPUs and many DSPs flush subnormals to zero anyway, so it is not there in practice.
concepts.L3: Precision degrades linearly through the subnormal range. The smallest fp32 subnormal $2^{-149}$ has one significant bit; $2^{-140}$ has ten. That is why they are a trap in low precision: fp16's subnormal range is only 10 binades wide, so a gradient of $10^{-8}$ lands at $5.96 \times 10^{-8}$ or below and carries at most one bit of information. Computed: rounding $10^{-8}$ to fp16 gives exactly $0.0$, because $10^{-8}$ is below half the smallest subnormal $2^{-24} = 5.96 \times 10^{-8}$. In bf16 the same value rounds to $1.0012 \times 10^{-8}$ with full 8-bit precision, because bf16's normal range reaches $1.18 \times 10^{-38}$. That single fact is most of the case for bf16.

L4.prompt_tpl: What does the value {v} become when rounded to fp16? And to bf16?
L4.explanation: Computed by exact round-to-nearest-even. fp16's smallest subnormal is $2^{-24} = 5.96 \times 10^{-8}$, so anything below $2.98 \times 10^{-8}$ flushes to zero. bf16 shares fp32's exponent range and keeps all three values as normals. This is the fp16-versus-bf16 argument in one table.

L4.prompt_tpl: Your CUDA kernel is compiled with flush-to-zero on and you compute d = x - y for two very close normals near {mag}. What guarantee is lost?
options: That d == 0 implies x == y
That d has the correct sign
That d is within one ulp of the true difference
L4.answer: That d == 0 implies x == y
L4.explanation: With subnormals, Sterbenz's lemma guarantees the difference of two nearby floats is exact, so a zero result means true equality. Flush-to-zero throws that away: distinct values can subtract to zero. Convergence loops written as while (x != y) can then terminate on a lie, or spin forever if the code tests the difference instead.

L0.body:
>>> import struct
>>> struct.unpack('>I', struct.pack('>f',  0.0))[0]   # 0x00000000
0
>>> struct.unpack('>I', struct.pack('>f', -0.0))[0]   # 0x80000000
2147483648
>>> 0.0 == -0.0
True
>>> 1.0/0.0
ZeroDivisionError        # Python raises; IEEE hardware returns +inf
>>> import numpy as np; np.float32(1.0)/np.float32(0.0)
np.float32(inf)          # 0x7F800000 ; -inf is 0xFF800000
>>> np.copysign(1.0, -0.0)
-1.0
L0.cloze: Positive and negative zero have {{c1::different bit patterns}} but compare {{c2::equal}}. Infinity is the encoding exponent field {{c3::all ones}} with significand {{c4::zero}}.

concepts.L1: Zero has two encodings that compare equal but are not interchangeable: $1/(+0) = +\infty$ and $1/(-0) = -\infty$. Infinity is the all-ones exponent with a zero significand, produced by overflow or by division by zero.
concepts.L2: Signed zero is a branch-cut marker, not a wart: it lets $\sqrt{}$, $\log$ and $\mathrm{atan2}$ approach a discontinuity from the correct side. The cost is that $x == 0$ does not tell you the sign, so a sign test must use $\mathrm{copysign}$ or $\mathrm{signbit}$.
concepts.L3: Overflow to infinity is silent by default and that is what bites in fp16. The largest fp16 is $65504$; the first fp16 value above it rounds to $+\infty$, so an attention logit or a residual accumulation of $10^{5}$ becomes $\mathrm{inf}$, then $\mathrm{inf} - \mathrm{inf} = \mathrm{NaN}$ on the next subtraction, and the loss goes to NaN with no error raised anywhere. Concretely: $\exp$ overflows fp16 at any argument above $\log(65504) = 11.09$, which is a completely ordinary attention logit. That is why softmax subtracts the row max first and why softmax is computed in fp32 even in a bf16 model.

L4.prompt_tpl: At what argument does exp(x) overflow to infinity in {fmt}?
L4.explanation: Computed as $\ln$ of each format's largest finite value. The fp16 threshold of $11.09$ is the entire reason softmax subtracts the row maximum: raw transformer logits routinely exceed $11$. bf16 and fp32 differ only in the fourth decimal place because they share an exponent field.

L4.prompt_tpl: A sorting routine deduplicates {n} float keys with a Python set() and then a separate pass compares bit patterns. The two passes disagree on exactly one pair. Which pair?
L4.answer: +0.0 and -0.0. They compare equal (so set() keeps one) but have different bit patterns (0x00000000 and 0x80000000).
L4.explanation: $\pm 0$ is the only pair in IEEE 754 that is equal but not bit-identical; NaN is the mirror case, bit-identical but never equal to itself. Any code that mixes value equality with bitwise identity will disagree on exactly these two.

L0.body:
# NaN = exponent all ones, significand NONZERO.
#   quiet NaN     : significand MSB = 1   e.g. fp32 0x7FC00000
#   signalling NaN: significand MSB = 0, rest nonzero  e.g. fp32 0x7F800001
# The remaining bits are the PAYLOAD - free space for diagnostics.
>>> import numpy as np, struct
>>> struct.unpack('>I', struct.pack('>f', float('nan')))[0]
2143289344                     # 0x7FC00000, the canonical quiet NaN
>>> float('nan') == float('nan')
False
>>> n = struct.unpack('>f', struct.pack('>I', 0x7FC0BEEF))[0]  # payload 0xBEEF
>>> n != n
True
L0.cloze: NaN is exponent {{c1::all ones}} with a {{c2::nonzero}} significand. The significand's top bit distinguishes {{c3::quiet}} from {{c4::signalling}}, and the remaining bits are the {{c5::payload}}.

concepts.L1: NaN encodes an invalid result: $0/0$, $\infty - \infty$, $\sqrt{-1}$. fp32 has $2 \times (2^{23}-1) = 16777214$ distinct NaN encodings; fp64 has $9007199254740990$. A quiet NaN propagates silently, a signalling NaN raises the invalid-operation exception on use.
concepts.L2: NaN is the only value not equal to itself, and that is the cheapest detector you have: `x != x` is one comparison with no library call and works on any type. The common mistake is testing `x == float('nan')`, which is always false and therefore never fires.
concepts.L3: The payload is 22 spare bits in fp32 and almost nobody uses them, but they are the right place for a poison value: encode which kernel produced the NaN, and it survives downstream because NaN propagation copies the payload on most hardware — recommended, not required, by IEEE 754-2019, so do not build a system that depends on it. The practical consequence of quiet-by-default is that a NaN born in layer 3 shows up as a NaN loss with no stack trace. That is why the debugging move is to turn signalling on — `torch.autograd.set_detect_anomaly(True)`, or `np.seterr(invalid='raise')` — and get an exception at the birth site instead of the death site.

L4.prompt_tpl: How many distinct NaN bit patterns does binary{w} have, and how many of those are quiet?
L4.answer: Total 2*(2^m - 1) where m is the significand width; half plus one are quiet: quiet = 2*2^(m-1) = 2^m. binary16: 2046 total, 1024 quiet. binary32: 16777214 total, 8388608 quiet. binary64: 9007199254740990 total, 4503599627370496 quiet.
L4.explanation: Both signs, exponent all ones, any nonzero significand: $2 \times (2^{m}-1)$. Quiet means significand MSB set, which leaves the lower $m-1$ bits free and always nonzero-qualifying: $2 \times 2^{m-1} = 2^{m}$. The count matters because it is the size of the payload space you could be using for diagnostics.

L4.prompt_tpl: A training loop guards against divergence with `if loss == float('nan'): break` after {n} steps. Why does it never fire?
L4.answer: NaN compares unequal to everything including NaN, so the == test is always False. Use loss != loss, math.isnan(loss), or torch.isnan(loss).
L4.explanation: IEEE 754 makes every comparison involving NaN false except `!=`. The idiom `x != x` is the portable one-comparison test and needs no import. This bug is common enough that it is worth grepping for `== float('nan')` and `== np.nan` in any codebase you inherit.

# IEEE 754-2019 defines five rounding-direction attributes:
#   roundTiesToEven      <- the default everywhere
#   roundTiesToAway      (ties away from zero; required for decimal)
#   roundTowardPositive  (ceiling)
#   roundTowardNegative  (floor)
#   roundTowardZero      (truncate; this is what a C cast does)
>>> round(0.5), round(1.5), round(2.5), round(3.5)   # Python round is RNE
(0, 2, 2, 4)
>>> import numpy as np; np.rint([0.5, 1.5, 2.5, 3.5])
array([0., 2., 2., 4.])
L0.cloze: IEEE 754 defines {{c1::five}} rounding attributes; the default is {{c2::roundTiesToEven}}. A C cast to int uses {{c3::roundTowardZero}}, which is {{c4::biased}} because its mean error is $-s/2$, not zero.

concepts.L1: Rounding is a defined operation, not an implementation detail: every basic operation must return the correctly rounded result, as if computed exactly and then rounded once. The default is round-to-nearest, ties-to-even.
concepts.L2: Ties-to-even is not aesthetic. Round-half-up has a mean error of $+s/2$ on exact halfway cases, so a long chain of roundings drifts steadily upward; ties-to-even splits them evenly and the drift cancels. Truncation is worse still: its mean error is $-s/2$ on all inputs, not just ties.
concepts.L3: Measured over the 10000 exact halfway values $i + 0.5$ for $i = 0 \ldots 9999$: round-half-up accumulates a total error of $+5000$, a mean bias of $+0.5$ per rounding; round-half-even accumulates exactly $0$. Truncation is the pathological one because the bias applies to every value, not one in $2^{m}$: quantising $10^{6}$ uniform samples to a grid of step $0.01$ gives a measured mean error of $-5.0 \times 10^{-3}$ under truncation, exactly $-s/2$, against $+8.9 \times 10^{-7}$ under round-to-nearest. Bias is the enemy in ML because it survives averaging over a batch, whereas variance does not — which is also the argument for stochastic rounding at very low precision.

L4.prompt_tpl: Round these to the nearest integer under roundTiesToEven: {vals}
L4.explanation: Verified with np.rint. Only exact halfway cases take the even branch; every other value rounds to the true nearest. Note round(2.5) == 2, which surprises people who learned round-half-up at school and is a frequent source of off-by-one differences between Python and other languages.

L4.prompt_tpl: Show that truncation toward zero has a mean error of -s/2 for positive inputs uniformly distributed over a grid of step s, while round-to-nearest has mean error 0.
L4.answer: Truncation error is -(x mod s), uniform on (-s, 0], mean -s/2. Round-to-nearest error is uniform on [-s/2, s/2], mean 0, variance s^2/12.
L4.explanation: Measured on $10^{6}$ uniform samples with $s = 0.01$: truncation mean error $-5.005 \times 10^{-3}$ and RMS $0.00578$; round-to-nearest mean $+8.9 \times 10^{-7}$ and RMS $0.00289$. Nearest halves the RMS and removes the bias. The $s^{2}/12$ variance reappears later as the quantisation-noise model.

L4.prompt_tpl: You accumulate {n} roundings of a value into a running total in a single format. Which rounding mode gives the smallest expected drift?
options: roundTowardZero, because it never overshoots
roundTiesToEven, because tie errors cancel and non-tie errors are already symmetric
roundTiesToAway, because it is symmetric about zero
L4.answer: roundTiesToEven, because tie errors cancel and non-tie errors are already symmetric
L4.explanation: Truncation biases every rounding by $-s/2$, so drift grows like $n \cdot s/2$. TiesToAway is symmetric about zero for a symmetric input distribution but still biases magnitude upward. TiesToEven is the only one with zero mean error on both ties and non-ties, so drift grows like $\sqrt{n}$ rather than $n$.

>>> import numpy as np
>>> np.finfo(np.float64).eps, np.finfo(np.float32).eps, np.finfo(np.float16).eps
(2.220446049250313e-16, 1.1920928955078125e-07, 0.0009765625)
# eps = 2^-m  (m = stored significand bits) = the gap from 1.0 to the next float
#   fp64 2^-52   fp32 2^-23   tf32 2^-10   fp16 2^-10   bf16 2^-7
#   fp8 e4m3 2^-3 = 0.125     fp8 e5m2 2^-2 = 0.25
# unit roundoff u = eps/2 = the max relative error of one rounding
L0.cloze: Machine epsilon is {{c1::$2^{-m}$}}, the gap between $1.0$ and the next representable number. Unit roundoff is {{c2::$u = \varepsilon/2$}}, the maximum {{c3::relative}} error of a single correctly-rounded operation.

concepts.L1: Machine epsilon is the distance from $1.0$ to the next representable float: $2^{-m}$ where $m$ is the stored significand width. fp64 $2.22 \times 10^{-16}$, fp32 $1.19 \times 10^{-7}$, fp16 and tf32 $9.77 \times 10^{-4}$, bf16 $7.81 \times 10^{-3}$.
concepts.L2: Two definitions circulate and they differ by a factor of two: the spacing above $1.0$ ($\varepsilon = 2^{-m}$, what numpy reports) and the unit roundoff ($u = 2^{-m-1}$, what error analysis uses). Papers say 'machine epsilon' and mean either. Check which one a bound assumes before you use it, or your error estimate is off by 2.
concepts.L3: Epsilon is a relative quantity, so it says nothing absolute. The gap below $1.0$ is $\varepsilon/2$, not $\varepsilon$, because $1.0$ sits at the bottom of its binade: measured in fp32, $1 - \mathrm{nextafter}(1,0) = 5.96 \times 10^{-8}$ while $\mathrm{nextafter}(1,2) - 1 = 1.19 \times 10^{-7}$. The useful reading is a digit count: $-\log_{10}(\varepsilon)$ gives roughly $15.95$ decimal digits for fp64, $7.22$ for fp32, $3.31$ for fp16 and tf32, $2.41$ for bf16, and $1.20$ for fp8 E4M3. bf16 carries between two and three decimal digits. That is the number to hold in your head when someone proposes storing a learning rate in it.

L4.prompt_tpl: Give machine epsilon and the approximate decimal digits of precision for {fmt}.
L4.explanation: $\varepsilon = 2^{-m}$ for stored width $m$; decimal digits are $(m+1)\log_{10}(2)$, counting the implicit leading bit. Computed exactly. The fp16 and bf16 numbers are the whole reason master weights are kept in fp32: a relative update of $10^{-4}$ is invisible in bf16.

L4.prompt_tpl: In fp64, what does (1.0 + {x}) - 1.0 evaluate to, and what is the relative error against {x}?
L4.explanation: Computed in fp64. Adding $x$ to $1.0$ forces $x$ onto the grid of spacing $\varepsilon = 2.22 \times 10^{-16}$; the subtraction is then exact but only recovers what survived. Below $\varepsilon/2$ the addition is a no-op and the result is exactly zero. This is the smallest possible demonstration of catastrophic cancellation.

concepts.L1: An ulp is the gap between adjacent floats at a given magnitude. It is a local, absolute quantity: $2^{-23}$ near $1.0$ in fp32 but $2.0$ near $1.7 \times 10^{7}$. Every binade $[2^{k}, 2^{k+1})$ holds exactly $2^{m}$ values, so the reals are sampled logarithmically.
concepts.L2: Epsilon is relative and ulp is absolute; conflating them produces tolerance code that is either useless or paranoid. `abs(a-b) < 1e-9` is meaningless near $10^{10}$, where one fp64 ulp is already $1.9 \times 10^{-6}$, and absurdly strict near $10^{-20}$. concepts.L3: The staircase is what makes floats useful and what makes them dangerous. Useful: constant relative precision across 277 binades in fp32, so the same code works on $10^{-30}$ and $10^{30}$. Dangerous: absolute precision collapses as magnitude grows. At $x = 2^{24} = 16777216$ in fp32 the ulp is exactly $2.0$, so adding $1$ is a no-op and a naive step counter silently stops advancing. The same mechanism kills naive summation: once a running total reaches magnitude $S$, any term below $\mathrm{ulp}(S)/2$ contributes nothing at all, and in fp32 that threshold is only $S \times 6 \times 10^{-8}$.

L4.explanation: Computed with np.nextafter. $\mathrm{ulp}(x) = 2^{\lfloor \log_{2}|x| \rfloor - 23}$: $1000$ is in the binade $[512, 1024)$ so the exponent is $9$ and the ulp is $2^{-14}$. At $2^{24}$ the ulp reaches $2$, which is where fp32 stops representing consecutive integers.

L4.prompt_tpl: A test asserts abs(expected - actual) < {tol} for fp32 values whose magnitude is around {mag}. Why is the test either vacuous or impossible?
L4.answer: At magnitude 1e7 one fp32 ulp is about 1.0, so any tolerance below that is impossible to satisfy. At magnitude 1e-25 one ulp is about 1e-32, so the tolerance is 7 orders of magnitude looser than the arithmetic and passes on nonsense.
L4.explanation: Absolute tolerances only make sense if you know the magnitude. The portable fix is a relative test with an absolute floor: `abs(a-b) <= rtol*max(abs(a),abs(b)) + atol`, which is exactly what numpy.allclose and torch.allclose implement, with atol covering the near-zero case where relative comparison degenerates.

concepts.t: Unit roundoff and the standard model of floating-point error

L0.body:
# The standard model (Higham, ASNA ch.2). For op in {+,-,*,/} and no over/underflow:
#
#     fl(a op b) = (a op b)(1 + delta),      |delta| <= u,     u = eps/2 = 2^(-m-1)
#
# Equivalently  fl(a op b) = (a op b)/(1 + delta')  with the same bound.
# u:  fp64 1.11e-16   fp32 5.96e-08   fp16 4.88e-04   bf16 3.91e-03
# Chained: prod (1 + delta_i) = 1 + theta_n  with |theta_n| <= n*u/(1 - n*u)
L0.cloze: The standard model says {{c1::$fl(a \circ b) = (a \circ b)(1+\delta)$}} with {{c2::$|\delta| \leq u$}}, where the unit roundoff $u$ is {{c3::$\varepsilon/2$}}. A chain of $n$ operations gives a factor bounded by {{c4::$nu/(1-nu)$}}.

concepts.L1: Every correctly-rounded operation returns the exact result times $(1+\delta)$ with $|\delta| \leq u = \varepsilon/2$. That single statement is the entire foundation of rounding-error analysis: it converts arithmetic into algebra you can bound.
concepts.L2: The model bounds relative error, so it says nothing when the exact result is near zero — which is exactly the cancellation case. It also assumes no overflow or underflow; in fp16 both assumptions fail routinely, which is why fp16 error analysis is not just fp32 analysis with a bigger $u$.
concepts.L3: The standard notation is $\theta_{n}$: a product of $n$ factors $(1+\delta_{i})^{\pm 1}$ equals $1 + \theta_{n}$ with $|\theta_{n}| \leq \gamma_{n} = nu/(1-nu)$, and for $nu < 0.1$ you can read $\gamma_{n} \approx nu$. This is why almost every bound in numerical linear algebra has the shape $\gamma_{n} \cdot \text{(something)}$: an inner product of length $n$ has backward error $\gamma_{n}$, a matrix product has $\gamma_{n}$, and LU with partial pivoting has $\gamma_{n}$ times a growth factor. The bound is worst-case: errors behave like a random walk, so observed growth is closer to $\sqrt{n} u$. Carry both, because the worst case is what an adversarial input hits.

L4.prompt_tpl: Give the unit roundoff u for {fmt}, and the worst-case relative error bound gamma_n for a summation of n = {n} terms.
L4.answer: fp32 u = 2^-24 = 5.9605e-08: n=1e3 -> gamma = 5.96e-05, n=1e6 -> 5.96e-02 (6 percent). bf16 u = 2^-8 = 3.9063e-03: n=1e3 -> nu = 3.9 > 1, bound vacuous; n=1e6 hopeless. Use the sqrt(n)*u estimate or a compensated algorithm.
L4.explanation: $\gamma_{n} = nu/(1-nu)$, which is only meaningful while $nu < 1$. The bf16 numbers show why bf16 is never used as an accumulator: at $n = 256$ the worst-case bound already exceeds unity. Tensor cores therefore accumulate in fp32 regardless of the input format.

L4.prompt_tpl: Derive the error bound for a length-n inner product computed left to right in a format with unit roundoff u.
L4.answer: Each product contributes one rounding and each of the n-1 additions contributes one, so the computed value is sum of x_i*y_i*(1 + theta_n) with |theta_n| <= gamma_n = n*u/(1-n*u). Hence |fl(x.y) - x.y| <= gamma_n * sum |x_i*y_i|.
L4.explanation: The bound is on $\sum |x_{i} y_{i}|$, not on $|\sum x_{i} y_{i}|$ — that gap is the condition number of the inner product. When the terms cancel, the relative error can be arbitrarily large even though the bound holds. This is the formal statement of why cancellation is dangerous.

>>> x = np.float32(1e6 + 1); y = np.float32(1e6 + 2)
>>> z = np.array([1e6+1, 1e6+2, 1e6+3, 1e6+4], dtype=np.float32)
>>> float(np.mean(z**2) - np.mean(z)**2)      # one-pass variance
65536.0
>>> float(np.mean((z - np.mean(z))**2))       # two-pass variance
1.25
>>> float(np.var(z.astype(np.float64)))       # truth
1.25
# Subtracting nearly-equal numbers is EXACT. What it destroys is the
# relative accuracy of whatever error was already sitting in the operands.
L0.cloze: Catastrophic cancellation happens when you subtract two {{c1::nearly equal}} numbers. The subtraction itself is {{c2::exact}}; what it destroys is the {{c3::relative}} accuracy of errors already present in the operands, by shifting them up into the leading digits.

concepts.L1: When $x$ and $y$ agree to $k$ leading bits, $x - y$ loses those $k$ bits of significance: the result is exact but has only $m - k$ meaningful bits left, and any prior error in $x$ or $y$ is amplified by $(|x|+|y|)/|x-y|$.
concepts.L2: The subtraction is not the bug. By Sterbenz's lemma, if $y/2 \leq x \leq 2y$ then $x - y$ is computed exactly. The damage was done earlier, when $x$ and $y$ were rounded; cancellation merely promotes that noise from the last bit to the first. Reformulate so the subtraction never happens.
concepts.L3: Watch it happen on the one-pass variance. Take $x = 10^{6} + \{1,2,3,4\}$ in fp32. The true variance is $1.25$. Computing $\mathbb{E}[x^{2}] - \mathbb{E}[x]^{2}$ requires squaring to about $10^{12}$, where one fp32 ulp is $65536$; the two terms then agree to roughly 12 digits and their difference is pure rounding noise. Measured result: $65536.0$, wrong by a factor of $52429$, and it can even come out negative. The two-pass form $\mathbb{E}[(x - \bar{x})^{2}]$ subtracts before squaring, keeps every intermediate near $2.5$, and returns exactly $1.25$. This is why every layernorm kernel uses a shifted or Welford update rather than the algebraically identical one-pass identity.

L4.prompt_tpl: Estimate how many significant decimal digits survive when you subtract two fp64 values that agree in their first {k} decimal digits.
L4.answer: About 16 - k. k=8 -> ~8 digits left. k=12 -> ~4 digits. k=15 -> ~1 digit.
L4.explanation: fp64 carries $\log_{10}(2^{53}) = 15.95$ decimal digits. Agreement in the first $k$ digits means those cancel, and the result is renormalised so the surviving $16 - k$ digits move into the lead, with garbage filling in behind. Verified: subtracting 1.2345678901234567 and 1.2345678901234000, which agree to 13 digits, leaves about 3 meaningful digits.

L4.prompt_tpl: A layernorm kernel computes variance as mean(x*x) - mean(x)**2 in fp32. On inputs centred near {mu} it returns a variance {n} times too large, sometimes negative. Diagnose and fix.
L4.answer: Catastrophic cancellation: both terms are around mu^2 and their difference is far smaller than one ulp at that magnitude. Fix by subtracting the mean first (two-pass), or by a Welford streaming update, or by accumulating in fp64.
L4.explanation: Measured on x = 1e6 + [1,2,3,4] in fp32: the one-pass identity returns $65536.0$ against a true $1.25$. A negative result is possible because the two large terms are each rounded independently. Two-pass returns exactly $1.25$. Welford gets the same accuracy in one pass at the cost of a division per element.

>>> a = np.full(10**6, np.float32(0.1))
>>> s = np.float32(0.0)
>>> for v in a: s = np.float32(s + v)     # naive left-to-right
>>> float(s)
100958.34375
>>> float(np.sum(a))                      # numpy: pairwise summation

>>> float(np.sum(a.astype(np.float64)))   # reference
100000.00149011612
# naive error bound ~ n*u ; pairwise ~ log2(n)*u ; both with the same u.
L0.cloze: Naive left-to-right summation has a worst-case relative error bound of {{c1::$nu$}}; pairwise (divide-and-conquer) summation has {{c2::$u\log_{2}n$}}. numpy's `sum` uses {{c3::pairwise}} summation, which is why it beats a Python loop over the same data.

concepts.L1: Naive summation adds each term into a growing accumulator, so the running total's ulp grows while the terms do not. Worst-case relative error is $\gamma_{n} \approx nu$. Pairwise summation recurses on halves and gets $u \log_{2} n$ for the same cost.
concepts.L2: The failure is not random noise, it is systematic absorption. Once the running sum exceeds $2 \cdot \mathrm{term}/u$, each new term rounds away entirely and the sum stalls. Shuffling the input does not fix it; sorting ascending helps a little; only changing the algorithm or the accumulator width actually fixes it.
concepts.L3: Measured on $10^{6}$ copies of fp32 $0.1$, true total $100000.00149$. The naive loop returns $100958.34$, relative error $9.58 \times 10^{-3}$ — nearly one percent, from an operation with no cancellation and no ill-conditioning at all. numpy's pairwise sum returns $100000.0078$, relative error $6.3 \times 10^{-8}$: five orders of magnitude better, same precision, same number of additions. Pairwise works because the tree has depth $\log_{2} n = 20$, so any single term passes through 20 roundings instead of up to $10^{6}$. The general lesson: an accumulator is the one place where the precision of the intermediate matters more than the precision of the data.

def kahan(xs):
    s = 0.0; c = 0.0                 # c carries the lost low-order bits
    for x in xs:
        y = x - c                    # apply the correction
        t = s + y                    # this rounding loses (y - (t - s))
        c = (t - s) - y              # recover exactly what was lost
        s = t
    return s

def neumaier(xs):                    # handles |x| > |s| correctly
    s = 0.0; c = 0.0
    for x in xs:
        t = s + x
        c += (s - t) + x if abs(s) >= abs(x) else (x - t) + s
        s = t
    return s + c                     # single final correction
L0.cloze: Kahan summation keeps a running compensation $c$ holding the {{c1::bits lost}} in the previous addition, recovered as {{c2::$(t-s)-y$}}. Neumaier's variant fixes the case where {{c3::the new term is larger than the running sum}} and applies the correction {{c4::once at the end}}.

concepts.L1: Compensated summation recovers the rounding error of each addition exactly and feeds it back. Kahan's version bounds the total relative error at $2u + O(nu^{2})$, independent of $n$ — a constant, not a growing, error.
concepts.L2: Kahan's $c = (t-s) - y$ is exact only when $|s| \geq |y|$. When a huge term arrives after a small running sum, the correction is computed on the wrong operand and is silently lost. Neumaier's branch on $|s| \geq |x|$ fixes exactly that case, which is why it is the one numpy and Julia ship.
concepts.L3: The textbook counterexample is $[1, 10^{100}, 1, -10^{100}]$, true sum $2$. Computed in fp64: naive gives $0.0$, Kahan gives $0.0$, Neumaier gives $2.0$, `math.fsum` gives $2.0$. Kahan fails because when $10^{100}$ arrives with $s = 1$, the quantity $(t - s) - y$ evaluates the correction against the large operand and returns zero. On well-behaved data Kahan is excellent: summing $10^{6}$ fp32 copies of $0.1$ it returns $100000.0$, relative error $1.5 \times 10^{-8}$ against the naive loop's $9.6 \times 10^{-3}$. The cost is four flops per element and a serial dependency that blocks vectorisation, so a wider accumulator is usually the better trade.

L4.prompt_tpl: Sum [1.0, {big}, 1.0, -{big}] in fp64 with naive, Kahan, and Neumaier summation. True answer is 2. Answer with the Neumaier result.
L4.answer: naive 0.0, Kahan 0.0, Neumaier 2.0. math.fsum also gives 2.0.
L4.explanation: Computed in fp64. Kahan's compensation term is exact only when the running sum dominates the incoming term; here the second element is $10^{100}$ times larger, so the recovered correction is zero and both ones are lost. Neumaier's magnitude test picks the other subtraction order and recovers them. This is the standard demonstration that Kahan is not unconditionally safe.

L4.prompt_tpl: Prove that c = (t - s) - y in Kahan's loop recovers the exact rounding error of t = s + y, assuming |s| >= |y|.
L4.answer: With |s| >= |y|, t = fl(s+y) and t - s is exactly representable (Sterbenz), so fl(t - s) = t - s. Then (t - s) - y is the exact amount by which t overshot s + y, again exactly representable. So c equals the rounding error of the addition, with no error of its own.
L4.explanation: This is the two-sum idea: for well-ordered operands the rounding error of a floating-point addition is itself a floating-point number and can be computed with three more additions. The condition $|s| \geq |y|$ is load-bearing, and dropping it is precisely how Kahan fails on the $10^{100}$ example.

concepts.L2: Rewriting the code cannot fix a badly conditioned problem; it can only stop you making things worse. Conversely a small condition number does not make a bad algorithm safe. concepts.L1: Backward error analysis reframes the question: instead of asking how wrong the answer is, ask how small a change to the input would make it exactly right. If that change is at the level of the input's own uncertainty, the algorithm has done everything possible.
concepts.L2: A tiny residual proves backward stability, not accuracy. Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting is backward stable, so its residual is always near machine level — including on a Hilbert matrix where the answer has no correct digits at all. concepts.L3: Measured on the $12 \times 12$ Hilbert system in fp64: the computed solution is off by $0.276$ in its worst component, yet the relative residual $\|b - H\hat{x}\| / (\|H\|\|\hat{x}\|)$ is $9.3 \times 10^{-17}$, below unit roundoff. #   worst case   : relative error grows like  L*u        (all errors align)
#   typical case : errors are independent, so like sqrt(L)*u  (random walk)

#   g = 1.05, L = 100  ->  131.5x       g = 0.90, L = 100 -> 2.66e-05

# as much as an optimisation one.

In bf16 with $u = 3.9 \times 10^{-3}$ and $L = 96$, the random-walk estimate is $3.8 \times 10^{-2}$ — large-sounding but harmless, since training is stochastic anyway. Those are the exploding and vanishing regimes, and they are properties of the architecture, not of the number format. This is why the fixes that actually work in deep networks are architectural — residual connections that force the gain near $1$, normalisation that rescales after each block, gradient clipping as a backstop — rather than precision upgrades.

scaled_loss = loss * S           # S = 2^15 = 32768, a power of two: exact

for p in params:
    p.grad /= S                  # unscale BEFORE clipping and before step
optimizer.step()
# A gradient of 1e-8:
#   unscaled in fp16 -> 0.0                     (rel error 1.0)
#   scaled by 2^15   -> 3.2759e-04 -> /S ->  9.9972e-09  (rel err 2.83e-04)

concepts.L2: It solves underflow only, and it buys that by spending overflow headroom. $S$ is bounded above by $65504 / g_{\max}$, so a single large gradient caps $S$ for the whole model. It is also why $S$ must be a power of two: any other value would round on multiply and again on unscale.
concepts.L3: The arithmetic, computed. A gradient of $10^{-8}$ rounds to exactly $0.0$ in fp16, a relative error of $1$. Scaled by $S = 2^{15} = 32768$ it becomes $3.2768 \times 10^{-4}$, a normal fp16 number; the round trip through fp16 and back gives $9.9972 \times 10^{-9}$, relative error $2.83 \times 10^{-4}$. The upper bound: if the largest gradient magnitude is $g$ then $S < 65504/g$, so $g = 10^{-2}$ allows $S$ up to $2^{22.6}$ and $g = 1$ allows only $2^{16}$. That window moves during training, which is the argument for making $S$ dynamic. bf16 needs none of this: its normal range reaches $1.18 \times 10^{-38}$, so $S = 1$ is correct.

L4.prompt_tpl: With loss scale S = 2^{k} and fp16, what is the largest gradient magnitude that will not overflow, and what is the smallest that survives as a normal number? Answer with the largest gradient magnitude that will not overflow.
L4.explanation: Computed from fp16's max 65504 and min normal $6.1035\times 10^{-5}$. The window is always exactly 40 binades wide; $S$ only slides it. That is the fundamental limit of loss scaling: it repositions the window, it cannot widen it.

L4.explanation: Order matters for every operation that is not homogeneous of degree one. The visible symptom is a loss plateau that starts shortly after an overflow event and has no other explanation.

#     E[SR(x)] = lo(1-p) + hi*p = lo + (hi-lo)p = x
#

L4.explanation: At $K = 4096$, $\sqrt{K} = 64$ and one fp16 ulp there is $0.0625$, so each unit-magnitude term is only 16 accumulator ulps. L4.prompt_tpl: Your fp8 GEMM at K = {K} produces results that differ from the bf16 baseline by more than expected. Which is the most likely cause?
options: The accumulator is fp32 in both cases, so the difference must come from the fp8 operand quantisation and its per-tensor scale
The fp8 accumulator is narrower than the bf16 one
fp8 GEMMs do not use tensor cores
L4.answer: The accumulator is fp32 in both cases, so the difference must come from the fp8 operand quantisation and its per-tensor scale
L4.explanation: Both paths accumulate in fp32, so accumulation is not the variable. What changed is that operands were rounded to 3 or 2 mantissa bits and rescaled by a per-tensor amax that may be stale if delayed scaling is in use. Check the amax history before suspecting the reduction.

L0.body:
# Affine (asymmetric):   q = clamp(round(x/s) + z, qmin, qmax)
#                        x_hat = (q - z) * s
#   s = (xmax - xmin) / (qmax - qmin)      z = round(qmin - xmin/s)
#
# Symmetric (z = 0):     q = clamp(round(x/s), -(2^(b-1)-1), 2^(b-1)-1)
#                        x_hat = q * s
#   s = amax / (2^(b-1) - 1)
#
# The three things you must record per quantised tensor:
#   the integer codes q, the scale s, and (if asymmetric) the zero-point z.
L0.cloze: Affine quantisation stores {{c1::$q = \mathrm{round}(x/s) + z$}} and dequantises as {{c2::$(q-z)s$}}. The scale $s$ is {{c3::the width of one integer step in real units}} and the zero-point $z$ is {{c4::the integer code that represents exactly 0.0}}.

concepts.L1: Quantisation maps a real range onto integer codes with a scale $s$ and an optional integer offset $z$. Dequantisation is $(q - z)s$. The whole design space is: how you pick $s$, whether you use $z$, and how many values share one $(s, z)$ pair.
concepts.L2: The zero-point must be an integer, not a float, and this is a correctness requirement rather than an efficiency one: padding, ReLU outputs and masked positions must dequantise to exactly $0.0$. A fractional zero-point would give every padded element a small nonzero value that then propagates through the GEMM.
concepts.L3: Work out what the integer kernel actually computes. For $y = \sum_{i} w_{i} x_{i}$ with $w_{i} = s_{w}(q^{w}_{i} - z_{w})$ and $x_{i} = s_{x}(q^{x}_{i} - z_{x})$, expanding gives $y = s_{w}s_{x} [\sum q^{w}q^{x} - z_{x}\sum q^{w} - z_{w}\sum q^{x} + N z_{w}z_{x}]$. The first term is the int8 GEMM you wanted; the second and third are correction sums that must be computed as well. If $z_{w} = 0$ (symmetric weights) two of the three correction terms vanish, and if both are symmetric all three do. That is the real reason production kernels use symmetric weights and reserve asymmetry for activations: symmetry is not more accurate, it is fewer instructions in the inner loop.

L4.prompt_tpl: A tensor has range [{lo}, {hi}]. Give the int8 asymmetric scale and zero-point using the full [-128, 127] code range. Answer with the scale s.
L4.explanation: Computed from $s = (x_{\max}-x_{\min})/(q_{\max}-q_{\min})$ and $z = \mathrm{round}(q_{\min} - x_{\min}/s)$. The rounding of $z$ to an integer means $0.0$ maps exactly to code $z$ but the endpoints may shift by up to half a step. For a non-negative range like [0,4] the zero-point sits at the bottom of the code range, which is the ReLU case.

L4.prompt_tpl: Expand the integer inner product for asymmetric weights and activations and show which correction terms disappear when the weight zero-point is zero.
L4.answer: y = s_w s_x [ sum(qw*qx) - z_x*sum(qw) - z_w*sum(qx) + N*z_w*z_x ]. With z_w = 0 the third and fourth terms vanish, leaving the int8 GEMM plus one per-output-channel constant z_x*sum(qw) that can be folded into the bias.
L4.explanation: This is why symmetric weight quantisation is near-universal: the surviving correction $z_{x}\sum q^{w}$ depends only on the weights, so it is precomputed once and folded into the bias, and the runtime kernel is exactly an int8 GEMM with an int32 accumulator. Asymmetric weights would need a per-input-row sum computed at inference time.

L0.body:
# How many values share one (scale, zero-point)?
#   per-tensor  : 1 scale for the whole weight matrix
#   per-channel : 1 scale per output row (folds into the bias for free)
#   per-group   : 1 scale per contiguous run of g weights (g = 128, 64, 32)
#
# Measured, 4096x4096 N(0,1), symmetric, relative L2 error:
#            per-tensor  per-channel  group-128  group-32
#   int8       0.01217     0.00868     0.00647    0.00535
#   int4       0.22070     0.15752     0.11734    0.09701
# Storage cost of group-g fp16 scales: 16/g bits/weight (g=128 -> 0.125 b)
L0.cloze: Granularity is how many weights share one scale. Going from per-tensor to group-32 cut measured int4 error from {{c1::0.2207}} to {{c2::0.0970}}, a factor of {{c3::2.3}}, at a storage cost of {{c4::$16/g$ bits per weight}}.

concepts.L1: Coarse scales are cheap to store and fast to apply; fine scales track local statistics. Per-channel is free at inference because the correction folds into the bias. Per-group costs $16/g$ extra bits per weight and is the standard for 4-bit.
concepts.L2: Granularity matters more than the choice of level placement. On the same Gaussian tensor, moving from per-tensor int4 to group-32 int4 cut the error by $2.3\times$, while switching the level placement from uniform to NF4 at fixed block size bought only $1.17\times$. Argue about block size first.
concepts.L3: The reason is that a scale is set by the block's extreme value, so a large block inherits the worst outlier in it. Plant a single value of $100$ in an otherwise $N(0,1)$ $4096 \times 4096$ matrix and measure the error on the untouched rows. Per-tensor int8: the scale jumps from $0.0421$ to $0.7874$ and the error on the other rows goes from $0.01217$ to $0.22736$, an $18.7\times$ degradation from one element in 16.7 million. Per-channel confines the damage to row 0, leaving $0.00868$. In int4 the per-tensor case is total: the scale becomes $14.29$ and the relative error on the rest is exactly $1.0$ — everything quantises to zero.

L4.prompt_tpl: A 4096x4096 N(0,1) weight matrix, symmetric int{b}. Give the relative L2 error for per-tensor, per-channel, group-128 and group-32.
L4.explanation: Measured with absmax scaling at each granularity. Each refinement roughly follows the shrinking expected block maximum: a smaller block has a smaller amax, hence a smaller step, hence less noise. The int4 per-tensor figure of 22 percent is why per-tensor int4 is never used in practice.

L4.prompt_tpl: One element of an otherwise N(0,1) 4096x4096 matrix is set to {v}. Give the per-tensor int{b} error on the remaining rows, with and without per-channel scaling.
L4.answer: int8: per-tensor error on rows 1+ rises from 0.01217 to 0.22736 (scale 0.7874); per-channel stays at 0.00868. int4: per-tensor error becomes exactly 1.00000 (scale 14.2857, everything rounds to zero); per-channel stays at 0.15752.
L4.explanation: Measured. A single outlier in 16.7 million elements degrades per-tensor int8 by 18.7x and destroys per-tensor int4 entirely. This is the mechanism behind every LLM quantisation failure and the reason granularity is the first knob to turn.

L4.prompt_tpl: You have {g} extra bits per weight to spend on 4-bit quantisation of a large model. What buys the most accuracy?
options: Move from uniform int4 levels to NF4 levels at the same block size
Halve the group size, spending the bits on more fp16 scales
Store the scales in fp32 instead of fp16
L4.answer: Halve the group size, spending the bits on more fp16 scales
L4.explanation: Measured on the same tensor: halving the group from 128 to 32 cut int4 error from 0.11734 to 0.09701 (17 percent), and the per-tensor to group-32 move is 2.3x. NF4 over uniform at fixed block size bought 14.6 percent. Scale precision is irrelevant: fp16 already resolves an absmax to four digits.

concepts.t: Quantisation noise and the 6 dB per bit rule

L0.body:
# Round to a uniform grid of step s: error is ~ U[-s/2, s/2]
#   E[e] = 0        Var[e] = s^2/12        RMS[e] = s/sqrt(12) = 0.28868 s
#
# SQNR = 20*log10(||x|| / ||x - x_hat||).  One extra bit halves s, so
#   SQNR gains 20*log10(2) = 6.0206 dB per bit.
#
# Measured on 4096x4096 N(0,1), per-tensor symmetric (amax = 5.350):
#   int8  s = 0.042127  predicted RMS 0.012161  measured 0.012161  38.30 dB
#   int4  s = 0.764301  predicted RMS 0.220635  measured 0.220635  13.12 dB
#   int7 32.21  int6 26.05  int5 19.74  int3 5.77  int2 0.11 dB
L0.cloze: Uniform rounding error has variance {{c1::$s^{2}/12$}} and RMS {{c2::$s/\sqrt{12}$}}. Each extra bit halves $s$, so signal-to-quantisation-noise ratio gains {{c3::$20\log_{10}2 = 6.02$}} dB per bit.

concepts.L1: Rounding to a uniform grid of step $s$ produces error that is close to uniform on $[-s/2, s/2]$: zero mean, variance $s^{2}/12$, RMS $0.2887 s$. Each additional bit halves $s$ and therefore adds $6.02$ dB of SQNR.
concepts.L2: The model assumes the signal spans many grid steps. It fails at very low bit widths, where the error is strongly correlated with the signal rather than uniform: at int2 the measured SQNR is $0.11$ dB, essentially no signal at all, and the additive-noise picture stops describing anything.
concepts.L3: Verified to five decimal places. On a $4096 \times 4096$ $N(0,1)$ tensor with per-tensor symmetric scaling, $\mathrm{amax} = 5.350$: int8 has step $0.042127$, predicted RMS $0.012161$, measured $0.012161$; int4 has step $0.764301$, predicted $0.220635$, measured $0.220635$. Measured SQNR by width: int8 $38.30$ dB, int7 $32.21$, int6 $26.05$, int5 $19.74$, int4 $13.12$, int3 $5.77$, int2 $0.11$. The consecutive per-bit gaps are $6.09$, $6.16$, $6.30$, $6.62$, $7.35$, $5.67$ going down from 8 bits — tight around the theoretical $6.02$ until the model breaks below 4 bits. Use it as a sanity check: an int8 weight tensor far below $38$ dB has an outlier or a granularity problem.

L4.prompt_tpl: An N(0,1) tensor with amax {amax} is quantised symmetrically to int{b}. Give the step, the predicted RMS error, and the SQNR in dB. Answer with the SQNR in dB.
L4.explanation: Predicted and measured RMS agreed to five decimals for int8 and int4 on a 4096x4096 draw. SQNR is $20\log_{10}(\|x\|/\|x-\hat{x}\|)$; for unit-variance $x$ that is $-20\log_{10}(\mathrm{RMS})$ up to the clipping correction.

L4.prompt_tpl: Derive the 6.02 dB per bit rule from the uniform-error model.
L4.answer: Noise power is s^2/12. Adding one bit halves s at fixed range, so noise power falls by 4 and SQNR rises by 10*log10(4) = 20*log10(2) = 6.0206 dB.
L4.explanation: Measured consecutive per-bit gaps on a Gaussian tensor, going down from 8 bits: 6.09, 6.16, 6.30, 6.62, 7.35, 5.67 dB — tight around theory until the uniform-noise model breaks below 4 bits. The rule is why 'int8 is enough, int4 is not' is roughly true: int8 leaves 38 dB of headroom, int4 leaves 13.

L0.body:
# The scale comes from an observed range. How you observe it is calibration.
#   min-max    : the absolute extreme seen. Zero clipping error, maximum
#                rounding error. One outlier ruins it.
#   percentile : clip at the 99.9th or 99.99th. Trades a little clipping
#                error for a much smaller step.
#   MSE        : grid-search the clip threshold to minimise ||x - x_hat||^2.
#   entropy/KL : minimise KL(P_fp || P_quant). TensorRT's int8 default.
# Needs a few hundred representative batches, no labels, no gradients.
# Wrong distribution in, wrong scale out.
L0.cloze: Calibration chooses the clipping range from observed data. {{c1::min-max}} has zero clipping error but the largest step; {{c2::percentile}} and {{c3::MSE}} deliberately clip outliers to shrink the step. The total error is {{c4::clipping error plus rounding error}}, and they trade against each other.

concepts.L1: Calibration is the process of choosing $s$ (and $z$) from data. The choice is a trade: a wider range clips nothing but makes the step large; a narrower range clips the tails but resolves the bulk better. Total error is the sum of both.
concepts.L2: Calibration data must match deployment. Scales calibrated on clean text and deployed on code, or calibrated at sequence length 512 and deployed at 32k, will be wrong — and wrong silently, since the model still produces fluent output. Activation ranges are the sensitive ones; weight ranges are fixed and can be read exactly.
concepts.L3: The trade is why min-max is rarely optimal. Clipping error is zero at min-max and rises as you narrow; rounding error falls as $s$ shrinks, linearly in the clip threshold. Their sum has an interior minimum, and for a Gaussian it sits well inside the observed range. On an $N(0,1)$ tensor the observed amax over 16.7 million samples was $5.35$, but almost all mass lies within $\pm 4$, so clipping at the $99.99$th percentile shrinks the step by about $25\%$. The order of operations: exact min-max for weights, which are static and can afford per-channel scales; MSE or percentile search for activations, whose tails are the entire problem.

L4.prompt_tpl: You calibrate int8 activation scales on {n} batches of clean English prose and deploy on source code. What is the failure mode?
options: The model raises an out-of-range error at inference
Activations exceed the calibrated range, get clipped, and the model degrades silently while still producing fluent output
Nothing: activation ranges are architecture-dependent, not data-dependent
L4.answer: Activations exceed the calibrated range, get clipped, and the model degrades silently while still producing fluent output
L4.explanation: Quantised kernels clamp; they do not signal. A distribution shift moves the activation tails outside the calibrated clip and every excursion saturates. Because language models degrade gracefully, this shows up as a small benchmark drop rather than a crash — which is why calibration-set coverage is checked, not assumed.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why the total quantisation error as a function of the clipping threshold has an interior minimum, and say which term dominates at each end.
L4.answer: Total error = clipping error + rounding error. As the threshold grows, clipping error falls to zero but the step s grows linearly, so rounding RMS s/sqrt(12) grows linearly. As the threshold shrinks, rounding error falls but clipping error grows with the tail mass beyond it. The sum is convex-ish with a minimum strictly inside the observed range for any distribution with tails.
L4.explanation: Min-max sits at the right-hand end where clipping is zero and rounding dominates; aggressive percentile clipping sits at the left where the reverse holds. MSE calibration simply grid-searches this curve. For heavy-tailed LLM activations the minimum is far from min-max, which is what makes activation quantisation hard.

L0.body:
# Above roughly 6.7B parameters, transformer activations develop systematic
# outlier FEATURES: a small set of hidden dimensions whose magnitude is
# 20-100x the rest, present in essentially every token.
#
# LLM.int8() (Dettmers et al. 2022): don't fight them, separate them.
#   1. per-row/per-column (vector-wise) int8 quantisation for the bulk
#   2. detect columns whose magnitude exceeds a threshold (default 6.0)
#   3. compute THOSE columns in fp16, the rest in int8, sum the two GEMMs
# Reported: >99.9% of values stay int8; fp16-level accuracy preserved at 175B.
L0.cloze: Large transformers develop {{c1::outlier features}}: a few hidden dimensions with magnitudes tens of times the rest, present in nearly every token. LLM.int8() handles them by {{c2::decomposing the matmul}}, keeping outlier columns in {{c3::fp16}} and the remaining {{c4::99.9 percent}} in int8.

concepts.L1: LLM activations are not Gaussian. Beyond about 6.7B parameters a handful of hidden dimensions carry values 20 to 100 times larger than the rest, consistently across tokens. Per-tensor activation quantisation therefore sets its scale from those dimensions and destroys everything else.
concepts.L2: The outliers are systematic, not noise: they occur in the same feature dimensions across inputs, and removing them destroys the model's accuracy, so they are load-bearing. That is why the successful methods isolate or rescale them rather than clipping them, and why activation quantisation is much harder than weight quantisation.
concepts.L3: The mechanism is the granularity result applied to activations. Planting a single value of $100$ in an $N(0,1)$ matrix raised per-tensor int8 error on the untouched rows from $0.01217$ to $0.22736$, and made per-tensor int4 error exactly $1.0$. Real LLM activations have hundreds of such dimensions. LLM.int8() sidesteps it by decomposition: sum the outlier columns in fp16 and the rest in int8, exact for the outliers and unpolluted for the bulk. The cost is a sparse fp16 GEMM alongside the dense int8 one plus per-batch outlier detection, so the speedup is modest and at small batch it can be slower than fp16.

L4.prompt_tpl: A 4096x4096 activation tensor is N(0,1) except for one entry of magnitude {v}. Give the per-tensor int8 scale and the relative error on the unaffected rows, with and without per-channel scaling. Answer with the per-tensor int8 scale.
L4.answer: amax becomes 100, so s = 100/127 = 0.7874 instead of 0.0421. Relative L2 error on the unaffected rows rises from 0.01217 to 0.22736, an 18.7x degradation. Per-channel scaling keeps them at 0.00868.
L4.explanation: Measured. One element in 16.7 million costs 18.7x accuracy under per-tensor scaling. In a real LLM the outliers are hundreds of dimensions appearing in every token, so this is a floor, not a worst case. The general lesson: an amax-based scale is a maximum statistic and maximum statistics are not robust.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why does LLM.int8() keep the outlier columns in fp16 rather than clipping them at the {p}th percentile?
options: Because clipping is slower than a separate GEMM
Because the outlier features are functionally important: clipping them costs large accuracy, so they must be represented exactly
Because fp16 GEMMs are faster than int8 GEMMs at these sizes
L4.answer: Because the outlier features are functionally important: clipping them costs large accuracy, so they must be represented exactly
L4.explanation: The paper's key empirical finding is that these dimensions are not noise — suppressing them degrades the model sharply. So the design must preserve their values while preventing them from setting the scale for everyone else. Decomposition does both; clipping does neither.

L0.body:
# Y = (X diag(t)^-1) (diag(t) W)  is algebraically identical to Y = X W.
# Choose the per-channel factor t to move range from activations to weights:
#     t_j = max|X_j|^a / max|W_j|^(1-a),      alpha typically 0.5
# X becomes easier to quantise, W becomes harder, and W had headroom.
# The scaling folds into the preceding layernorm at build time -> free.
#
# Result: W8A8 (both weights AND activations int8) becomes viable, so the
# GEMM is a real int8 GEMM with no fp16 side path.
L0.cloze: SmoothQuant rewrites $XW$ as {{c1::$(X\,\mathrm{diag}(t)^{-1})(\mathrm{diag}(t)\,W)$}}, an {{c2::algebraically identical}} product, choosing $t$ to move dynamic range from the {{c3::activations}} to the {{c4::weights}}. The rescaling is folded into the preceding {{c5::layernorm}}, so it costs nothing at inference.

concepts.L1: SmoothQuant observes that activations are hard to quantise and weights are easy, then moves the difficulty. A per-input-channel factor divides the activations and multiplies the weights, leaving the product unchanged, and is absorbed into the previous layer's parameters.
concepts.L2: Unlike LLM.int8() this leaves the GEMM shape intact: no second sparse kernel, no per-batch outlier detection, so W8A8 runs as a plain int8 matmul. The price is that it is a static, calibration-time transform — if deployment activations put outliers in different channels, the migration is misaimed.
concepts.L3: The exponent $\alpha$ controls where the difficulty lands. At $\alpha = 0$ nothing moves; at $\alpha = 1$ the activation channel maxima are fully equalised and the weights absorb the entire spread, which can make the weights the bottleneck. The paper's $\alpha = 0.5$ splits it geometrically: $t_{j} = \sqrt{\max|X_{j}| / \max|W_{j}|}$, so both sides end with maxima proportional to $\sqrt{\max|X_{j}|\max|W_{j}|}$. It works because of the granularity asymmetry: weights tolerate per-channel scales, whereas activation scales must be per-tensor or per-token, since the channel dimension is the GEMM's reduction dimension and cannot be factored out of the sum.

L4.prompt_tpl: Show that the SmoothQuant transform leaves the layer output unchanged, and explain why per-channel activation scales cannot be used instead.
L4.answer: (X diag(t)^-1)(diag(t) W) = X diag(t)^-1 diag(t) W = X W since diagonal matrices commute with their own inverse. Per-channel activation scales fail because the channel index is summed over in Y_ik = sum_j X_ij W_jk; a factor s_j inside the sum cannot be pulled out, so the int32 accumulator cannot be rescaled by a single constant afterwards.
L4.explanation: This is the structural reason activation quantisation is harder than weight quantisation, and it is worth being able to state precisely. Weight scales can be per-output-channel because the output index is free; activation scales must be per-token or per-tensor because the input-channel index is contracted.

L4.prompt_tpl: With alpha = {a}, an activation channel max of {x} and a weight channel max of {w}, give the SmoothQuant factor t and the post-transform maxima on both sides. Answer with the factor t.
L4.answer: t = x^a / w^(1-a). x=64, w=0.25, a=0.5: t = 8/0.5 = 16; activation max becomes 64/16 = 4, weight max becomes 0.25*16 = 4. x=100, w=1.0: t = 10/1 = 10; activation max 10, weight max 10. At alpha=0.5 both sides land on sqrt(x*w).
L4.explanation: Computed from the definition. At $\alpha = 0.5$ the two maxima are equalised at the geometric mean $\sqrt{x \cdot w}$: $\sqrt{64 \times 0.25} = 4$ and $\sqrt{100 \times 1} = 10$. That is the balanced split; other $\alpha$ values bias the difficulty toward one side.

L0.body:
# AWQ (Lin, Tang, Tang et al., MLSys 2024 best paper):
#   the salient weights are the ones multiplied by LARGE ACTIVATIONS,
#   not the ones with large magnitude.
#
#   1. measure per-input-channel activation magnitude on a calibration set
#   2. scale up the weight channels that see large activations by s_j,
#      compensating in the activations, then quantise
#   3. grid-search s_j to minimise the output error of that linear layer
#
# Weight-only (W4A16): activations stay fp16, so no activation quantisation.
# Reported: protecting ~1% of weights recovers most of the quality.
L0.cloze: AWQ identifies salient weights by the magnitude of the {{c1::activations they multiply}}, not by their own magnitude. It scales those weight channels {{c2::up}} before quantising so they land on {{c3::finer relative steps}}, compensating in the activations. It is a {{c4::weight-only}} method: activations remain fp16.

concepts.L1: AWQ is weight-only 4-bit quantisation that chooses per-input-channel scales by looking at activation statistics. Scaling up a weight channel before rounding reduces its relative quantisation error; the compensating down-scale is folded into the previous op.
concepts.L2: The counterintuitive part is that weight magnitude is the wrong saliency signal. A large weight multiplied by a near-zero activation contributes nothing to the output, while a small weight in a channel that sees an outlier activation dominates it. AWQ measures the activation side and protects accordingly.
concepts.L3: The mechanism is simple once stated. Under group-wise absmax quantisation the relative error of a weight is roughly $s/(2|w|)$ for group step $s$; multiplying a channel by $\lambda > 1$ before quantisation raises $|w|$ without much raising the group amax, provided that channel was not the group maximum, so its relative error falls by roughly $\lambda$. AWQ picks $\lambda_{j}$ per input channel from calibration activation magnitudes, then grid-searches one exponent to minimise the layer's output MSE — no backpropagation, no Hessian, no weight updates. Contrast: LLM.int8() raises the precision of outliers, SmoothQuant moves range to the weights, AWQ spends resolution where output is sensitive.

L4.prompt_tpl: In a linear layer, weight w1 = {a} multiplies an input channel whose typical magnitude is 0.01, and w2 = {b} multiplies a channel with typical magnitude 50. Which weight should AWQ protect?
options: w1, because it has the larger magnitude
w2, because its contribution to the output is larger despite its small magnitude
Neither: saliency is determined by the group amax
L4.answer: w2, because its contribution to the output is larger despite its small magnitude
L4.explanation: Contribution to the output is $w \cdot x$: $2.0 \times 0.01 = 0.02$ against $0.05 \times 50 = 2.5$, over a hundred times larger. Quantisation error in $w_{2}$ is amplified by the same factor of 50 in the output. This is AWQ's core observation and why it beats magnitude-based saliency.

L4.prompt_tpl: Contrast LLM.int8(), SmoothQuant and AWQ as three answers to the LLM outlier problem, in one sentence each.
L4.answer: LLM.int8(): keep the outlier columns in fp16 and decompose the GEMM. SmoothQuant: migrate range from activations to weights with a per-channel factor folded into layernorm, enabling W8A8. AWQ: leave the ranges alone but scale up the weight channels that see large activations so the grid resolves them better, weight-only W4A16.
L4.explanation: All three accept that outliers are load-bearing and cannot be clipped. They differ in what they change: the kernel (LLM.int8), the parameterisation (SmoothQuant), or the allocation of grid resolution (AWQ). Knowing which one a deployment uses tells you what its failure mode will be under distribution shift.

# GPTQ (Frantar, Ashkboos, Hoefler, Alistarh 2022): quantise a layer's
# weights one column at a time, and after each column push the error it
# introduced into the columns not yet quantised.
#
#   objective : minimise || W X - W_hat X ||_2^2  per layer, X = calibration acts
#   Hessian   : H = 2 X X^T   (of that quadratic; layer-local, not the model's)
#   update    : after fixing column q, W_remaining -= (w_q - q_q) * H^-1 row

# Uses a Cholesky of H^-1, processes in blocks of 128 columns, no gradients.
# Reported: 175B params quantised to 3-4 bits in about four GPU hours.
L0.cloze: GPTQ minimises the {{c1::layer output error}} $\|WX - \hat{W}X\|_{2}^{2}$ rather than the weight error. It quantises {{c2::one column at a time}} and pushes the resulting error into the {{c3::not-yet-quantised}} columns using the inverse Hessian {{c4::$H = 2XX^{T}$}}.

concepts.L1: GPTQ is post-training weight quantisation that minimises the layer's output error, not its weight error, using the exact Hessian of that quadratic objective. Each column is rounded, and the error is compensated by adjusting the remaining columns.

L0.body:
# PTQ: quantise a trained model. Needs calibration data, no labels, minutes
#      to hours. GPTQ, AWQ, SmoothQuant, NF4 are all PTQ.
# QAT: simulate quantisation during training so the weights adapt to it.
#      Needs the training pipeline, labels, and real compute.
#
# QAT's problem: round() has derivative 0 almost everywhere, so no gradient
# reaches the weights. Straight-through estimator (STE): pretend it is
# the identity on the backward pass.
#
#   forward :  x_hat = s * clamp(round(x/s), qmin, qmax)
#   backward:  dL/dx = dL/dx_hat * 1[qmin*s <= x <= qmax*s]   # 1 inside, 0 outside
L0.cloze: PTQ quantises an {{c1::already-trained}} model using calibration data; QAT {{c2::simulates}} quantisation during training so weights adapt. QAT needs the {{c3::straight-through estimator}} because $\mathrm{round}$ has {{c4::zero derivative almost everywhere}}.

concepts.L1: PTQ takes a trained model and a few hundred calibration batches. QAT inserts fake-quantise nodes into training so the weights learn to be robust to rounding. PTQ is cheap and usually enough at 8 bits; QAT wins at 4 bits and below and for small models.
concepts.L2: The straight-through estimator is a lie that works: the true gradient of a step function is zero wherever it exists, so STE substitutes the identity inside the clipping range and zero outside. The clamping term matters more than people expect — without it, saturated weights keep receiving gradient and drift further out.
concepts.L3: The decision is usually budget, not accuracy. At int8 with per-channel weight scales, PTQ typically lands within a fraction of a percent of the float baseline on a large model, so QAT buys nothing for real cost. Below 4 bits, or on architectures with little redundancy such as MobileNet-style depthwise layers, PTQ degrades sharply and QAT recovers most of it. LLMs sit oddly: too expensive to train for full-model QAT, and so over-parameterised that PTQ works better than it has any right to — which is why the LLM quantisation literature is almost entirely PTQ.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why quantisation-aware training needs the straight-through estimator, and write down the backward pass including clipping.
L4.answer: round() is piecewise constant, so its derivative is 0 wherever it exists and undefined at the step points; a true gradient would be zero and no learning would happen. STE defines dL/dx = dL/dx_hat inside the representable range and 0 outside: dL/dx = dL/dx_hat * 1[qmin*s <= x <= qmax*s].
L4.explanation: The clipping indicator is not optional. Without it a weight pushed past the clip threshold keeps receiving gradient in the direction that pushed it there, drifts further out, and stays saturated. With it, saturated weights get zero gradient and the clipping range effectively becomes a hard boundary.

L4.prompt_tpl: You must ship a {n}B-parameter LLM at 4 bits. PTQ or QAT?
options: QAT, because 4 bits is below the threshold where PTQ works
PTQ (GPTQ or AWQ): full-model QAT at this scale costs a training run, and PTQ at 4 bits with group-wise scales is close enough
Neither: use 8-bit PTQ instead, since 4-bit is not viable for LLMs
L4.answer: PTQ (GPTQ or AWQ): full-model QAT at this scale costs a training run, and PTQ at 4 bits with group-wise scales is close enough
L4.explanation: The classical PTQ-fails-below-8-bits result comes from small, efficient vision models with little redundancy. Large language models are heavily over-parameterised and tolerate 4-bit weight-only PTQ with group-wise scales. QAT would cost a full training run for a small marginal gain, which is why the entire LLM quantisation literature is PTQ.

# Three separate sources, often conflated:
#  1. ATOMICS. atomicAdd on a float commits in hardware arrival order,
#     which depends on scheduling. Different order, different rounding.
#  2. SPLIT-K / TILE COUNT. A GEMM's reduction tree follows the tile
#     decomposition, which follows the shape and the kernel heuristic.
#     Change the batch size, change the tree.
#  3. AUTOTUNING. cuDNN/cuBLAS benchmark candidates at runtime and
#     cache a winner, which can differ between processes.
# Measured: np.sum over 200 permutations of 2^20 fp32 values gave

concepts.L1: A GPU reduction is non-deterministic when the order in which partial sums combine is not fixed. Atomics order by hardware arrival; split-K GEMMs order by tile decomposition; autotuners choose the decomposition at runtime. None of it is a bug.
concepts.L2: The usual explanation, 'threads race', is one third right and misleads people into seeding more RNGs. Two of the three sources are deterministic per shape and vary only when the shape or the tuning cache changes — which is why the same script gives identical results twice and different ones after a batch-size change.
concepts.L3: The batch-size case is the operationally important one and the least intuitive: a kernel is not batch-invariant if its reduction tree depends on the number of tiles, so an inference server that dynamically batches will return slightly different logits for the same prompt depending on what else was in flight. Small — until it crosses an argmax boundary and a different token is emitted.

The spread is tiny in relative terms (1.8e-06) and irrelevant to training, but it is a hard floor on bit-reproducibility.

The fix is batch-invariant kernels whose reduction order does not depend on how many other sequences are in the batch, not more seeding. concepts.L1: A NaN in the loss says nothing about where it came from, because NaN propagates silently through every subsequent operation. The technique is to bisect the graph with finiteness assertions until you find the first tensor that is not finite.
concepts.L2: Check for inf as well as NaN, and check earlier than you think. The usual chain is overflow to inf first, then $\mathrm{inf} - \mathrm{inf}$ or $\mathrm{inf}/\mathrm{inf}$ producing NaN one or two ops later, so the tensor that first goes non-finite is an inf and the NaN you noticed is already downstream of the real event.
concepts.L3: A short ordered checklist beats a debugger. Same step every rerun? Then it is data or a deterministic overflow; log the batch and replay it. Loss scale collapsing? Then gradients really are overflowing and the model is diverging. Forward or backward? A forward hook that raises tells you in one run. Common birth sites by frequency: $\log$ of a value that reached zero, division by a variance or norm that underflowed, $\exp$ of a logit above $88.7$ in fp32 or $11.09$ in fp16, a masked-attention $-\infty$ that made a whole softmax row $-\infty$, and $\sqrt{}$ of a negative variance from the one-pass identity. Four of those five are cancellation or overflow.

L4.prompt_tpl: An attention implementation masks disallowed positions with -inf. On sequences where an entire row is masked, the loss becomes NaN at step {n}. Trace it.
L4.answer: A fully masked row is all -inf. Softmax subtracts the row max, which is -inf, giving -inf - (-inf) = NaN for every element; even without the max trick, exp(-inf) = 0 for all entries and the denominator is 0, so the division is 0/0 = NaN. Fix by masking with a large finite negative value (e.g. -1e9 in fp32, or the format's most negative finite value scaled) or by skipping fully masked rows.
L4.explanation: This is the single most common NaN in transformer code and it is a pure IEEE consequence: $\infty - \infty$ and $0/0$ are both defined to be NaN. It typically appears only on the one batch that contains a fully padded sequence, which is why it can survive thousands of clean steps before firing.

L4.prompt_tpl: Your loss is NaN at step {n}. Which first move localises the problem fastest?
options: Lower the learning rate and restart
Register forward hooks asserting torch.isfinite on every module output, and rerun to the failing step
Switch the whole model to fp32
L4.answer: Register forward hooks asserting torch.isfinite on every module output, and rerun to the failing step
L4.explanation: The hooks name the first non-finite tensor, which is the information you lack; the other two options change the symptom without identifying the cause and cost a full rerun each. Lowering the learning rate may hide a genuine bug, and fp32 may hide an overflow that will return the moment you go back to half precision.
